and mining no less than for manufacturing. To convince this House, if need be, that my statement is in keeping with the campaign in my section of the province;, I would read briefly a description of the^ platform upon which one of the candidates appealed to his electorate:
In reiterating his stand for Maritime rights, he stated the Maritimes had plenty of coal and the necessary products and manufactories to produce fuel and steel for the whole country, but these were not being utilized while the country was paying out huge sums to import the same materials from the United States, all because of the meddling and tinkering with the tariff by the Mackenzie King group.
In reference to the coming federal campaign, he said all the petty canvasses would be swept aside by the big issues, which will be the development of our own natural resources for our own people, the supplying of necessary raw materials for our manufactures, traffic for our transportation systems, employment for our own people and markets for our own agriculturists.
Those were the salient points upon which we appealed to the electorate-and you have the results. In 1921 Nova Scotia sent what was known as "the solid sixteen" to support the government; New Brunswick sent five Liberals, five Conservatives and one Progressive; Prince Edward Island sent their "solid four" to support the administration. In the last election the "solid sixteen" dwindled to three; and let me say, Mr. Speaker, en passant, that there might have been another cabinet casualty had the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Macdonald) taken the plunge in his own county of Pictou. But as discretion is always the better part of valour, he left Pictou behind and ran in the comparatively safe constituency of Antigonish-Guysborough. New Brunswick returned ten Conservatives to one Liberal, and even the lone Progressive who was the potato champion of the last parliament, camouflaged as a Liberal-Progressive candidate in Victoria-Carleton, failed to secure election. I am sure that he must feel sorry for ever allying himself with the Liberals in that county. In Prince Edward Island we made an even split -fifty-fifty. What was the reason for this decisive change in the opinion of the electorate of the Maritime provinces? It has been so fully discussed by my hon. friend for Cumberland (Mr. Smith) and my colleague for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming) that I need not dwell upon that question further.
In connection with the Maritime provinces the leader of this government, speaking at Kentville, Nova Scotia, during the last campaign said that he knew not what Maritime rights were; he knew not what the grievances of the Maritime provinces were. He asked someone to tell him what their rights were so that he could fight for them. In answer we said we gave him twenty-five 
out of thirty-one members in 1921 and that they must have been as dumb as oysters ii they had not enlightened him. We sent somebody to tell him. In formulating the scheme of confederation it was recognized that the geographical disadvantage oif the Dominion could only be overcome by the federal government as a national undertaking. The Intercolonial railway, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railway were all constructed with federal assistance, with the intention of overcoming this geographical disadvantage. But the intent and spirit of confederation has been lost sight of and Canadian traffic has been diverted to foreign channels, which diversion is detrimental to the best interests of Canada and the empire and is sorely felt by the people of the Maritime provinces. Those representing the provinces near the Atlantic come here and appeal to this House again, as they have appealed during the last four years without effect. But we have this much to say: our own leader, instead of duplicating the action of Mr. Mackenzie King in telling 'he people of Nova Scotia that he knew not what Maritime rights were, -admitted that he knew what they were and was prepared to consider them if elected.
We believe that the natural resources of our provinces-no more in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick than in the province of Alberta- should foe developed. The bituminous coal deposits of the Maritime provinces and those in Alberta should be exploited to create an all-Canadian fuel policy Which would not leave us at the mercy of anthracite coal strikes in the United States. We say that when you expend $119y000,000 of good Canadian money in importing bituminous coal from the United States you are not giving a fair show to the coal areas of Alberta and the Maritimes. In developing the natural resources and in wiping out that huge freight rate existing between Winnipeg and Moncton, in giving the transcontinental railways a Chance to transport our products from the western prairies to the port of Quebec in summer months and the ports of St. John and Halifax during the closed season, you will fulfil -a part of the obligation undertaken by the Fathers of Confederation in 1867. We sacrificed at that time our natural market; we sacrificed a natural outlet in order to develop a bigger and broader Canada. We expected to create in this northern hemisphere a united Canada over whioh the British flag would fly, reaching from ocean to ocean and from the Arctic to the southern boundary. But we find to-day, possibly owing to political

exigencies, that we are divided into three different sections. We have the Maritimes in the east, the provinces of Quebec and Ontario towards the centre, and the prairie provinces in the west. Why can we not have a policy of equalization off conditions, giving fair play to every portion of the Dominion and rectifying some of the errors made in the past?
I have just mentioned the province of Quebec, and I know hon. members opposite will say: "We have no one in the province of Quebec to support the policy of your right hon. leader." They will try to convey the impression throughout this broad land that Quebec does need protection. It would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, if you could get together, say, in Le 'Monument National, Montreal, the electors of the constituencies of St-Denis, Ste-Marie, St-Jaoques, Maisonneuve and St-Henri and have there discussed the fiscal questions of to-day by the leaders of the political groups. If you could there take a referendum upon the advisability of putting into effect a protective tariff you would find 95 per cent of those constituents voting for such a system. But evidently the great question of protection is overshadowed by other petty matters.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the result of the last election after all, is not so discouraging to my right hon. leader. In the provincte of Quebec the Liberals in 1921 polled 554,000 votes while the Conservatives polled 144,000. In the last election the Liberals polled 469,000 votes, and the Conservatives 273,000, a reduction of 84,861 to the Liberal party and a gain of 129,743 to the Conservative party. My hon. friends will say "You have not much to show for it." I quite agree. We have only been Successful in detaching four from the solid bloc of 65, but mind you, there were determined efforts made in several constituencies which prevented us from getting more. I do not want my French-speaking friends from Quebec to rise to-morrow and say that I have slandered their fair province, for I am of the same blood. I respect their traditions as I want them to respect mine. I have in my hand this evening evidence showing the unfair and partial manner in which my right hon. leader was treated by some of the newspapers of that province. My leader spoke the other afternoon when moving his resolution, and in the evening the acting leader of the government, the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), in reply to my leader, said:

connection with the closing of factories. I have too much respect for the province of Quebec to think that such tactics would change one vote, but at the same time the attempt was made. House to house canvasses were carried on, and circulars distributed in direct contravention of the Elections Act, because they did not have printed on the bottom the name of the printer, which the present law requires, and then hon. gentlemen opposite come here and tell us that the only question discussed in the province of Quebec was protection and the tariff.
I have spoken of the coal situation, and some hon. members of this House may wonder why, in the last parliament the very large delegation representing the Maritime provinces and supporting the government did not support a national coal policy. On the 16th of March, 1925, a resolution was moved in this House by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) which read in part as follows:
-that no part of Canada should be left dependent upon the United States for such (coal) supply. . . That a duty should be placed on coal from the United States to ensure an all-British supply for Canada and thus afford adequate protection.
That resolution was discussed for some time, but shortly after ten o'clock in the evening a representative from the Maritime provinces moved an adjournment of the debate, well knowing that that meant placing the motion at the bottom of the list of private members' resolutions, and that if parliament had sat for fifteen months the resolution would then never be reached again. We demanded a vote upon it, and practically every member from the Maritime provinces supporting the government voted closure on the coal question, voted to prevent hon. members of this House from expressing an opinion as to the advisability of developing a national policy on coal for this Dominion. But, Mr. Speaker, those members on the other side of the House who so vbted contrary to their own interests and the interests of the part of the country they represented, were found among the fallen on the battlefield, and we have now with us a new contingent of men, who are prepared to discuss and do their utmost to forward the rights of the Maritime provinces, at the same time not overlooking the interests of the other provinces of this Dominion.
